title: TGW1a locus simultaneously shortens growth duration and boosts grain yield in rice.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: No data file exists to open. I confirmed by API that the paper is closed access with no deposited data: Europe PMC core record (isOpenAccess=N, inEPMC=N, hasSuppl=N, hasData=N, hasDbCrossReferences=N, no dataLinksTagsList); Unpaywall (oa_status 'closed', best_oa_location null, has_repository_copy false); Semantic Scholar (openAccessPdf status CLOSED). NCBI esearch returned 0 hits in BioProject and 0 in GEO for TGW1a/OsFTL1; elink from PMID 42623462 returned no database cross-links; Zenodo returned 0 records. The Science landing page and the expected supplementary PDF both returned HTTP 403 (publisher block).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the study's content comes from the 150-word abstract plus a commentary summary: a quantitative trait locus (a genome region affecting a measured trait) qTGW1a encoding a flowering-locus-T-like protein; effects of 3.67-8.67 days shorter growth duration and 4.22-11.00% higher grain yield in five modern cultivars and their first-generation hybrids. A web search quoted the data availability statement as 'All raw data are available in the main text or the supplementary data S1', i.e. no repository deposit; I could not retrieve that statement directly because the article is paywalled.

a1_downloadable.note: Closed access with no public deposit of any kind. Unpaywall reports oa_status 'closed' and no repository copy; Europe PMC has no full text, no supplement and no data cross-references; BioProject, GEO and Zenodo searches returned zero hits. The only data (supplementary data S1) sits behind a Science subscription and the publisher returns HTTP 403 to any automated request.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Not checked, because no file is reachable. From the abstract, the candidate labels (days to heading, thousand-grain weight, grain yield per plot) would be measured columns in a field-trial table, so A2 would probably pass if the table could ever be obtained.

a3_inputs_present.note: Not checked. Promoter sequence variants would likely be described in text or figures rather than supplied as sequence; the Nipponbare reference genome would supply sequence for any coordinates given, which is routine.

a4_units_stated.note: Not checked. The abstract's units (days, percent yield) are conventional and clearly stated, so this would likely pass.

a5_enough_rows.note: No row count seen, and the abstract points to a very small n: five modern cultivars plus derived first-generation hybrids, in field trials. Even with a mapping population of chromosome segment substitution lines (typically ~100-200 lines) and a haplotype survey of a few hundred accessions, this is far below the ~1,500-row bar. A5 would very likely fail even with full access.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: unknown; almost certainly a few spreadsheets (<10 MB)
a6_fits_laptop.note: Not checked. Size is not the problem here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Not checked; nothing to compare the paper against.

a8_label_provenance.note: Not checked. The labels would be direct field and laboratory measurements (heading date, grain weight, nitrogen content), not another model's output, so A8 would pass on provenance grounds.

existing_models.name: deepCRE / DeepPlantCRE (deep learning models that predict gene expression level from plant promoter DNA sequence)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported in search results as >80% accuracy classifying high vs low expression from flanking regions across Arabidopsis, tomato, sorghum and maize, with cross-species held-out testing; DeepPlantCRE claims 1.6-3.8% accuracy gain over pure convolutional models. Numbers read from search snippets, not from the papers themselves.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Cross-species transfer of the regulatory code is named as the open problem in the DeepPlantCRE abstract snippet; I did not read the discussions.

existing_models.name: AgroNT and PlantCaduceus (plant DNA language models used for regulatory annotation and variant-effect prediction)
existing_models.score_and_split: Search snippets describe AgroNT predicting promoter/terminator strength and tissue-specific expression, and PlantCaduceus identifying causal variants in Arabidopsis and maize. No specific metric or split verified.

existing_models.name: Genomic selection benchmark for rice grain-yield traits (ridge regression best linear unbiased prediction plus machine learning and deep learning models on 688 accessions, 66,456 haplotype markers)
existing_models.score_and_split: Search snippet reports 17 models compared for grain length, grain width and thousand-grain weight; ridge regression best linear unbiased prediction was most robust. Accuracy values not verified.

existing_models.name: Rice heading-date prediction models combining crop growth models with machine learning (Frontiers in Genetics 2020; dual-ensemble approach 2024)
existing_models.score_and_split: Snippets report machine learning with genotype markers beating crop growth models for heading date at tested sites; no verified metric or split.

backbone.name: AgroNT or PlantCaduceus (plant DNA language models), or AlphaGenome for regulatory-variant effects
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU would suffice for embedding a few hundred promoter sequences, if any sequences were available.
backbone.licence: AgroNT and PlantCaduceus weights are openly downloadable; AlphaGenome is non-commercial. Not relevant here because there is no data to attach a head to.

integration.partner_dataset: 3,000 Rice Genomes Project variants plus the Rice SNP-Seek phenotype database, joinable to this locus on genomic coordinates (Os-Nipponbare-Reference-IRGSP-1.0, chromosome 1 near LOC_Os01g11940)
integration.join_key: genomic coordinates plus accession identifier (IRIS ID)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does promoter haplotype at flowering-time genes predict heading date and grain weight across thousands of sequenced rice accessions better than genome-wide marker models do? - but that question can be asked entirely from the public 3,000 Rice Genomes and SNP-Seek resources and needs nothing from this paper.

controls.positive_control: Would have been: recover the known large effects of Ghd7 and Hd1 haplotypes on heading date, which are textbook in rice.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling; not runnable, no labels exist.
controls.external_validation: Rice SNP-Seek / 3,000 Rice Genomes phenotype panels would serve, but only for a project built on public data rather than on this paper.

honest_claim_h3: No claim is possible from this paper's own data: the only tables are behind a subscription, and the described experiment covers five cultivars, so any model fitted to it would describe one breeding programme's field trials and nothing more.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use rice promoter DNA variants to predict how many days a plant takes to flower and how heavy its grain is.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would show the model the DNA sequence of a flowering-gene promoter for each rice variety, plus which version (haplotype) of the neighbouring grain-number gene it carries. The number of varieties in this paper is unknown and probably under 100.
plain_idea.predict: Days from sowing to heading (when the flower head emerges) and thousand-grain weight in grams, both measured by hand in replicated field plots by the authors.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Rice breeders choosing parent lines want to know in advance whether a promoter change will shorten the season without costing yield; a working predictor would save a field season per cross. Even a failure would show how far sequence alone can go for a trait this environment-dependent.

more_or_better_data.why: Existing rice trait predictors are trained on 688 to 2,265 sequenced accessions (the 688-accession genomic selection benchmark and 3,000 Rice Genomes subsets). This paper offers field data on five cultivars and their hybrids - three orders of magnitude less.

confidence_score.why: Field trials of this kind do have replicate plots and multiple years, which in principle support an error estimate, but I could not open any table to confirm replicates exist or how many, so no calibration claim can be made.

models_beatable.why: The heading-date machine learning papers date from 2020 and 2024 and the grain-weight genomic selection benchmark found that plain ridge regression best linear unbiased prediction won, which suggests headroom for modern DNA language models. But beating them needs the large public panels, not this paper.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition outright: we cannot obtain this paper's data at all, so it cannot be added to any baseline's inputs.

ml_idea: Considered and dropped: predict rice heading date and thousand-grain weight from flowering-gene promoter haplotypes, with a plant DNA language model (AgroNT or PlantCaduceus) frozen and a small regression head fitted. The idea is reasonable, but it must be built on the public 3,000 Rice Genomes Project and Rice SNP-Seek phenotype panels, not on this paper, which contributes no obtainable data.

effort.compute_note: Not estimated; no data file was reachable, so there is nothing to size.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Query Unpaywall and Europe PMC for the DOI before anything else - 'oa_status: closed, has_repository_copy: false, hasData: N' killed this candidate in two minutes.

verdict_reason: Part A1 fails: closed-access Science paper with no public deposit anywhere (Unpaywall closed, no BioProject, no GEO, no Zenodo, supplement returns HTTP 403), and the data availability statement points only to a paywalled supplementary file. A5 would almost certainly fail too - the study's phenotypes cover five cultivars and their hybrids, not the ~1,500 rows needed. The interesting prediction question (promoter haplotype to heading date and grain weight) is better served by the public 3,000 Rice Genomes and Rice SNP-Seek panels, which several 2020-2025 models already use.
